draft:
The trick of this version of **Flagpole Sitta** is how calm it sounds while the narrator comes apart. A synth pad holds long, sustained chords. A drum machine keeps a steady mid-tempo pulse, kick on every beat, snare on two and four, hi-hats ticking along. A bass synth loops a simple line. Over that, AWOLNATION and Elohim sing in a breathy, slightly processed voice pitched fairly high, with a second vocal layer stacked on the main one, all of it wrapped in clean reverb. Nothing lurches. The song is a list of nerves, paranoia and contempt, and the production carries it like a slow walk through a bright hallway.

That gap is where the feeling lives. The narrator never admits to being in trouble outright. The closest the song comes is the chorus: "I'm not sick but I'm not well." It's a half-confession, the kind you give when someone asks how you're doing and the honest answer would take too long. Everything around it is armor. There's a sneer at people who breed and people who own TVs, a brag about piercing a tongue that "doesn't hurt." There's a crack that anyone who's bored must be boring. The jokes work as a guard. The repeated "okay..." asides land like shrugs, a way of laughing before anyone else can.

But the cracks show. The verses slide from self-inspection, staring into a mirror at "the rottenness and evil in me," to blame. Someone told them all he was crazy and got him committed, and then the grammar turns on itself: "You killed my mind." It starts as a wish to shut off his own head and ends as an accusation. Pride and fear sit together and never settle. He wants to go underground with the moles, and he still wants you to watch him go.

Then there's the guilt tucked into the second chorus: "And it's a sin to live so well." Nothing else in the song admits comfort. It's a strange thing to hear next to a narrator who says he's in hell, and the song doesn't explain it. Maybe the misery is real and also a little bit chosen. The lyric leaves both open.

The wish list in the middle, publishing 'zines and raging against machines, reads like a scene the narrator wants to belong to and mocks at the same time. In this cover it's sung softly, without irony, and that makes it sound almost wistful. The song closes on a count-off, "one, two, three, four," as if the band were about to start over.

The song lets you hear someone joke their way through a breakdown in a voice gentle enough that you notice, under the joking, that he's asking for help.
